# Introduction

`r Biocpkg("gamdid")` is an R/Bioconductor package for **differential
distribution (DD) analysis** in single-cell data. Conventional
differential abundance methods focus exclusively on detecting mean shifts
between experimental conditions. `gamdid` is designed to detect *any* form of
distributional difference (shape and mean differences).

## Key features

* **GAM workflow** The sample space of each feature is discretized
    into a histogram, and a Poisson generalized additive model (GAM) is
    fitted per group using `r CRANpkg("mgcv")`. A Wald-type chi-squared test
    on the group-specific smoothing splines yields a p-value for inferring
    any type of distributional difference both in location and in shape,
    referred to as the GAM p-value.
* **P-value aggregation** To increase the power to detect distributional
    changes that are strongly driven by differences in the mean, the p-value
    obtained from the GAM is combined with a p-value derived from the
    `r Biocpkg("msqrob2")` framework via the harmonic mean p-value
    [@Wilson2019]
* **Nuisance correction** The nuisance effect (e.g. batch or MS run) is
    removed from the data before GAM fitting, so the shape test focuses on
    the covariate of interest.
* **Multi-group testing** For covariates with more than two groups,
    `gamdid` performs an omnibus test followed by post-hoc pairwise
    comparisons, with multiple testing correction via stagewise testing
    (`r Biocpkg("stageR")`) or Benjamini–Hochberg FDR [@BH_procedure].
* **Interpretable visualization** `visFit` overlays the fitted GAM densities
    on the empirical histograms and marks the differential regions of the
    distribution with grey shading, directly linking the visualization to
    the inference.

## Workflow overview

The typical `gamdid` workflow has three steps:

1. `compDistr()` — fit GAMs and run the distributional comparison.
2. `topFeatures()` — extract and rank the most significant features.
3. `visFit()` — visualize the fit for individual features of interest.

`gamdid` integrates seamlessly with the standard Bioconductor single-cell
proteomics infrastructure: both `SummarizedExperiment` /
`SingleCellExperiment` objects and the `QFeatures` multi-assay format are
supported.

# Installation

To install the development version from GitHub:

```{r install_gh, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("remotes")
}

remotes::install_github("statOmics/gamdid")
```

# Load packages

```{r load_packages}
library(gamdid)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

# Example data

We use the `pe` dataset bundled with `gamdid`, a small subset of the
pSCoPE dataset from @Leduc2022 obtained via `r Biocpkg("scpdata")`.

```{r load_data}
data(pe)
pe
```

The object contains log-transformed protein intensities for
`r nrow(pe)` proteins and `r ncol(pe)` cells. The `colData` slot records
the relevant experimental variables:

```{r coldata}
table(pe$SampleType)
table(pe$Set)
```

`SampleType` (Melanoma vs. Monocyte) is the biological covariate of interest;
`Set` identifies the MS run and will be treated as a nuisance variable.

# Two-group differential distribution analysis

## Running `compDistr`

The main function is `compDistr`. We compare the protein intensity
distributions between Melanoma and Monocyte cells, correcting for the MS run
effect:

```{r compDistr_two}
pe_dd <- compDistr(
    object    = pe,
    covariate = "SampleType",
    nuisance  = ~ (1 | Set)
)
```

## Inspecting the results

Results are stored in the `rowData` of the returned object. For a two-group
comparison, a single column of adjusted p-values is added, named after the
contrast:

```{r results_two}
head(rowData(pe_dd)[, "SampleTypeMelanoma_VS_SampleTypeMonocyte", drop = FALSE])
```

The `metadata` slot stores summary information about the analysis:

```{r metadata_two}
metadata(pe_dd)
```

`adj_alpha` is the Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted significance threshold: the
largest per-feature threshold at which at most 5% of called features are
expected to be false positives (the BH step-up threshold).

## Adjustment strategies for two-group comparisons

The `adjust` argument controls how multiple testing correction is applied.
For a two-group comparison, `adjust = "stagewise"` and
`adjust = "contrastwise"` are equivalent — both apply Benjamini–Hochberg FDR
correction to the single pairwise comparison column.

Setting `adjust = "none"` skips multiple testing correction entirely and
returns raw p-values in three separate columns: `_GAM` (GAM test),
`_msqrob2` (msqrob2 test), and `_aggregated` (harmonic mean of the two).
This is useful for exploratory analysis or when you intend to apply your own
correction.

```{r compDistr_none}
pe_dd_none <- compDistr(
    object    = pe,
    covariate = "SampleType",
    nuisance  = ~ (1 | Set),
    adjust    = "none"
)
head(rowData(pe_dd_none))
```

The three raw p-value columns share the contrast name as a prefix:
`_GAM` contains the GAM test p-value, `_msqrob2` the msqrob2 test
p-value, and `_aggregated` their harmonic mean combination.

## Ranking features with `topFeatures`

`topFeatures` extracts the most significant features from the `rowData` and
returns them as a sorted `data.frame`. For a two-group comparison, it
automatically sorts by the single pairwise comparison column:

```{r topFeatures_two}
topFeatures(pe_dd)
```

When `adjust = "none"` is used, `topFeatures` requires you to specify
`sort.by` explicitly:

```{r topFeatures_none}
topFeatures(pe_dd_none,
    sort.by = "SampleTypeMelanoma_VS_SampleTypeMonocyte_aggregated"
)
```

## Visualizing individual features


```{r vis_hist}
#| fig.cap: >
#|   Histogram overlay with differential region shading for the most
#|   significant feature.
top_features <- rownames(topFeatures(pe_dd, n = 10))
visFit(pe_dd, feature = top_features[1], plot = "hist")
```

`visFit` produces an interpretable plot for a chosen feature. The default
`plot = "hist"` overlays the normalized histograms and GAM-fitted densities
for both groups. Grey shading marks regions where the two densities differ
significantly at the `adj_alpha` threshold stored in `metadata`. The default
`adj_alpha`is the Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted significance level from the 
inference step. The shading can therefore be seen as a second stage 
in the stagewise testing procedure after the original inference:
it localizes *where* in the distribution the significant difference occurs.
If you wish to use a different threshold, pass it via the `alpha` argument:

```{r vis_alpha, eval=FALSE}
visFit(pe_dd, feature = top_features[1], plot = "hist", alpha = 0.05)
```

The alternative `plot = "diff"` adds a second panel showing the
log-ratio of the two fitted densities (the *difference smoother*) with
confidence bands. Regions where the confidence band excludes zero are
shaded:

```{r vis_diff}
#| fig.cap: >
#|   Two-panel plot showing the empirical densities (top) and the difference
#|   smoother (bottom).
visFit(pe_dd, feature = top_features[1], plot = "diff")
```

`visFit` returns plot(s), so you can assign and reuse them:

```{r vis_assign, eval=FALSE}
p <- visFit(pe_dd, feature = top_features[1], plot = "hist")
```

# Multi-group analysis (more than two conditions)

When the covariate of interest has more than two levels, `compDistr`
automatically performs an omnibus test (testing whether *any* pair of groups
differs) followed by all pairwise post-hoc comparisons.

Here we use the `Field` variable from the `pe` dataset (four levels) to
illustrate the multi-group workflow:

```{r compDistr_multi}
pe_multi <- pe[, !is.na(pe$Field)]
pe_multi$Field <- as.factor(pe_multi$Field)

pe_dd_multi <- compDistr(
    object = pe_multi,
    covariate = "Field",
    nuisance = ~ (1 | Set),
    adjust = "stagewise"
)
```

## Adjustment strategies for multi-group comparisons

`gamdid` offers three adjustment strategies for multi-group analyses.

`adjust = "stagewise"` (used above) applies a two-stage procedure via
`r Biocpkg("stageR")`: in the first stage, the omnibus p-value is adjusted
across features with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control. Only features that
pass this screening stage proceed to the second stage, where the pairwise
comparisons are adjusted for multiple testing across the comparisons via the
Holm method,
within each significant feature.

`adjust = "contrastwise"` applies Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction
independently to the omnibus column and to each pairwise comparison column.

`adjust = "none"` skips correction entirely. It returns three raw p-value
columns, `_GAM`, `_msqrob2` and `_aggregated`, for the omnibus test and for
every pairwise comparison. For the four levels of `Field` (six pairwise
comparisons) this gives 3 x 7 = 21 columns per feature.

```{r compDistr_multi_contrastwise, eval=FALSE}
pe_dd_multi_cw <- compDistr(
    object    = pe_multi,
    covariate = "Field",
    nuisance  = ~ (1 | Set),
    adjust    = "contrastwise"
)

## FDR-corrected omnibus and per-contrast columns are all available
head(rowData(pe_dd_multi_cw))
```

## Results for the multi-group analysis

```{r results_multi}
head(rowData(pe_dd_multi))
```

## Ranking features with `topFeatures`

For a multi-group result, `topFeatures` automatically sorts by the
`"omnibus"` column:

```{r topFeatures_multi}
topFeatures(pe_dd_multi)
```

To sort by a specific pairwise comparison instead, supply `sort.by`
explicitly:

```{r topFeatures_multi_pairwise}
topFeatures(pe_dd_multi, sort.by = "Field1_VS_Field2", n = 5)
```

When `adjust = "none"` is used, `topFeatures` requires an explicit `sort.by`
since there are multiple raw p-value columns with no unambiguous default:

```{r topFeatures_multi_none, eval=FALSE}
topFeatures(pe_dd_multi_none, sort.by = "omnibus_aggregated")
```

## Visualization for multi-group comparisons

`visFit` returns one plot per pairwise comparison as a named list:

```{r vis_multi, fig.height=5}
#| fig.cap: >
#|   Pairwise GAM density comparisons for the most significant feature in
#|   the multi-group analysis.
top_multi <- rownames(topFeatures(pe_dd_multi, n = 10))
visFit(pe_dd_multi, feature = top_multi[1], plot = "hist")
```

# Tips and best practices

* **Minimum observations** The default `minObs = 50` requires at least 50
    non-missing values per group before fitting a GAM. In experiments with
    few cells per condition, lowering this threshold may increase the number
    of tested features at the cost of less stable GAM fits. Features below
    the threshold get an `NA` p-value: they are not tested at all, also not
    with the msqrob2 mean test alone.
* **Number of bins** The default `bins = 25` works well for most datasets.
    Increase `bins` if you suspect fine-grained distributional differences;
    decrease it if many features have marginal counts per bin.
* **Nuisance variables** Always account for technical variation (MS runs,
    batches) via the `nuisance` argument.
* **Visualization** Use `visFit(..., plot = "diff")` to understand *where*
    in the distribution the groups differ, which aids biological
    interpretation.
